title: Atomism from the 17th to the 20th Century

summaries.example: Imagine breaking a toy block into smaller pieces. An atomist asks whether this breaking could go on forever, or whether matter finally reaches tiny pieces that cannot be broken by nature. Later scientists used experiments, such as watching tiny specks move in liquid, to test ideas about such particles.
summaries.summary: Atomism is the view that matter is made from very small particles. In the seventeenth century, philosophers such as Robert Boyle used this idea to explain ordinary things, such as color, heat, and the strength of objects, by the shapes, sizes, and movements of hidden particles. Other thinkers used “natural minima,” tiny parts suited to particular substances and chemical changes. These ideas were interesting, but experiments did not strongly confirm them. Newton added forces to particle theories, making them more flexible but also raising new questions about what forces really are. During the nineteenth century, chemical formulas and the kinetic theory of gases connected particle ideas with measurements. Experiments on Brownian motion later showed patterns that matched the movement of molecules. By the early twentieth century, atoms and molecules were accepted as part of experimental science, although science still had more to discover about their inner parts and laws.
key_ideas: Seventeenth-century thinkers revived the ancient idea that material things are made from tiny particles.
Some atomists thought atoms had only shape, size, and motion. Others gave tiny parts special properties connected with particular substances.
Philosophical arguments alone did not settle whether atoms or empty space really existed.
In the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, chemistry, the motion of gases, and Brownian motion gave much stronger experimental support for atoms.
Modern science accepted atoms through experiments and theories, not only through a general philosophical guess.
summaries.why_it_matters: The history of atomism shows how philosophy and science can work differently. Philosophy can ask what matter must be like and whether an idea is clear. Science tests ideas with measurements and experiments. The story also teaches that a theory may be useful before it is well supported, and that strong evidence can change how people understand the smallest parts of matter.

important_terms.definition: The idea that matter is made from extremely small particles, often called atoms.
A tiny part of matter that an atomist treats as a basic building piece.
Empty space between pieces of matter. Some thinkers said moving matter needs this space.
A careful test or observation used to learn about the natural world.
A way of explaining something by showing how it comes from simpler parts.

questions_to_think_about: How could anyone learn about things too small to see directly?
Why might two explanations fit the same experiment?
What is the difference between a useful idea and a proven idea?
Would you call a tiny particle a basic building block if scientists later found smaller parts inside it?

summaries.example: Suppose a theory says that gas pressure comes from countless molecules colliding with the walls of a container. If the theory merely renamed the gas laws, it would add little evidence for molecules. The kinetic theory was more significant because it connected molecular motion with pressure, diffusion, viscosity, and predictions about gases under changing conditions. Its difficulties, including the problem of explaining specific heats, did not disappear. Later, Perrin’s measurements of Brownian particles produced values for Avogadro’s number that agreed with several independent methods, strengthening the case that molecules were real.
summaries.summary: The modern history of atomism concerns both a theory of matter and a debate about scientific knowledge. Seventeenth-century mechanical atomists proposed that material reality consists of atoms moving in a void. They sought to reduce observable qualities to a few primary properties, but their arguments from clarity and intelligibility did not establish that atoms or void existed. Natural-minima theories pursued a different goal: explaining chemical combination through substance-dependent least parts. Newtonian atomism added mathematically developed mechanics and forces, but atomic forces remained difficult to justify independently of the phenomena they explained. Nineteenth-century chemistry created productive formula-based practices and laws of proportion. These practices could be interpreted atomistically or more cautiously as descriptions of combining amounts, so their epistemic significance remained disputed. The kinetic theory of gases went further by deriving measurable gas behavior from molecular motion and collisions, although it faced problems involving specific heats and reversibility. Thermodynamics offered powerful non-atomistic explanations of thermal and chemical phenomena. Brownian-motion experiments, especially Jean Perrin’s measurements, connected several independent phenomena through molecular assumptions and yielded mutually consistent estimates of Avogadro’s number. By the early twentieth century, belief in atoms had become scientifically secure, but a complete account of matter still required discoveries about subatomic structure and quantum mechanics.
key_ideas: Mechanical atomism aimed at a general account of material reality in terms of atoms in a void, with properties such as shape, size, and motion. Its support was largely philosophical rather than experimental.
Natural-minima theories addressed chemical combination and allowed substance-specific properties, so they differed from mechanical atomism in both purpose and ontology.
Newtonian theories added forces and mechanics, but forces created questions about the intelligibility and empirical basis of atomic properties.
Daltonian chemistry connected atomic hypotheses with combining weights and chemical formulas, yet formulas could often be used without a commitment to literal atoms.
The kinetic theory of gases gave atomism explanatory and predictive power, while thermodynamics provided a successful rival that did not require microscopic particles.

Perrin’s studies of Brownian motion and his mutually agreeing measurements of molecular quantities made the molecular-reality interpretation highly compelling, though atomism still did not explain every property of matter.
summaries.why_it_matters: Atomism provides a case study in scientific realism: how, and when, should unobservable entities be accepted as real? It also separates two claims that are easy to confuse. One is that particles exist and help explain observable behavior. The stronger claim is that a specified particle theory completely explains all material properties. The historical evidence strongly supported the first claim by the early twentieth century, while the second remained unfinished. The episode therefore illuminates the changing boundary between philosophical metaphysics, scientific explanation, and experimental confirmation.

important_terms.definition: A theory claiming that matter consists of fundamental or near-fundamental particles whose combinations and motions produce larger-scale properties.
An account of material reality that explains observable qualities through the arrangements and motions of small particles.
The problem of inferring the nature of unobservable particles from experiments on observable matter.
A proposed smallest part of a substance, often used in early theories of chemical combination rather than as a universal building block of matter.
A theory explaining gas behavior through the statistical motions and collisions of molecules.
A scientific approach that describes regularities in observable quantities without requiring a microscopic account of matter.
The irregular movement of microscopic particles suspended in a fluid, later used as evidence for molecular motion.
A number representing the quantity of particles in a specified amount of substance; historically, its measurement helped test molecular theories.

questions_to_think_about: What kind of evidence could justify belief in entities that cannot be directly observed?
Does a theory gain support merely by explaining known laws, or must it also predict new results?
Why did chemical formulas support chemistry even when some chemists did not interpret them atomistically?
How can a statistical theory allow apparent violations of a law such as the second law of thermodynamics?
Does confirming atoms require confirming a complete theory of matter?

summaries.example: Think about a sealed bicycle pump. When air is squeezed into a smaller space, the pressure rises. A kinetic theory explains this by imagining many molecules moving and hitting the pump’s walls. Faster or more frequent collisions can produce greater pressure. This is different from simply writing down a rule about pressure: the theory tries to connect the rule to hidden motion. Scientists still had to test whether its predictions matched measurements.
summaries.summary: Atomism is the idea that matter is built from tiny particles. Ancient Greek versions were revived in the seventeenth century, but early modern thinkers developed several different forms. Mechanical atomists, including Robert Boyle, imagined atoms with basic features such as shape, size, and motion, moving through a void. They hoped to explain qualities like color, heat, and elasticity through particle arrangements. Their arguments made the picture seem understandable, but experiments did not yet show that atoms existed. Natural-minima theories were different: they proposed smallest parts belonging to particular substances and used them to think about chemical combination. Newton’s mechanics and the idea of forces expanded atomism, although forces themselves were difficult to connect clearly to tiny particles. In the nineteenth century, chemistry produced laws and formulas that could be used with or without belief in atoms. The kinetic theory of gases made a stronger case by explaining pressure, diffusion, and other effects through molecular motion, while also facing challenges from thermodynamics. Finally, experiments on Brownian motion showed that suspended particles moved in ways expected if they were being struck by invisible molecules. Agreement among several measurements helped make atomic theory part of accepted science.
key_ideas: Early modern atomists disagreed about what particles were like and what they were meant to explain.
Mechanical atomism tried to explain all material properties using atoms, empty space, and motion. Natural-minima theories focused more narrowly on substances and chemical change.
Newton’s use of forces made particle theories more powerful, but it also raised questions about whether forces were clear, basic features of matter.
Chemical formulas became useful tools for organizing chemical reactions, even though scientists disagreed about whether the symbols proved that atoms were real.
The kinetic theory of gases gained support because it explained familiar gas laws and predicted additional results, though it had important problems.
Brownian motion gave especially strong evidence because measurements of particle movement agreed with values obtained from other kinds of experiments.
summaries.why_it_matters: This history helps us understand how scientific ideas earn support. A clever philosophical picture is not automatically an established scientific theory. Scientists need links between ideas and observations, including predictions that rival explanations do not easily match. Atomism also shows that one word can cover different theories: some versions were broad metaphysical views, while later versions were specialized scientific models.

important_terms.definition: The view that matter is made of tiny particles, and that larger things depend on how those particles are arranged and move.
A very small particle proposed as a basic part of matter in a particular theory.
Empty space, which some atomists believed was needed for particles to move.
A smallest part of a substance, often used to explain chemical changes and combinations.
A theory that explains gases through the movement and collisions of many molecules.
A way of explaining a complicated feature by showing how it comes from simpler parts.
Evidence or knowledge about things that cannot be observed directly.
The random-looking motion of tiny particles floating in a liquid or gas.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a scientist prefer an explanation with hidden particles over a description of what can be measured?
Can a theory be useful even if it is not yet strongly confirmed?
Why could two different theories sometimes explain the same observation?
What makes evidence from Brownian motion stronger than an unsupported guess about atoms?
If atoms have smaller parts, are atoms still useful building blocks?
